Date: 2027-06-02 16:15 PT | Duration: 58m | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes
Attendees: Jordan Ellis (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Dr. Lena Ortiz (CTO, Wintergreen), Samir Patel (Infra Lead), Hannah Cho (Security), Evan Myers (ML Engineer)
summary: Discovery focused on how Wintergreen Labs can run Redwood Private in an air-gapped facility. Key concerns: secure offline updates, hardware compatibility (older GPU fleet + limited NVMe), image signing/verification, patch windows, and auditability (KMS, HSM, SOC2 artifacts). Redwood AE/SE outlined update packaging options, signed image delivery, and mitigations (staged rollouts, local fallback to quantized variant). Agreed next steps: send runbook, HW checklist, schedule on-site workshop, provide test artifact.
topics: Intro / current infra -> Air-gap update mechanics -> Hardware constraints -> Security controls (KMS/HSM, SSO, audit logs) -> Rollout strategy and rollback -> Commercial/pricing signals
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Ellis: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we know time is tight so we'll try and get through constraints, update model, and ops. Quick intros?
[00:10] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Lena here, CTO at Wintergreen, we run imaging pipelines and some clinical inference, big compliance focus.
[00:15] Samir Patel: Samir, infra lead, we manage on-prem racks across two secure facilities, mostly older T4/V100 style GPUs but prepping a rack upgrade later this year.
[00:22] Hannah Cho: Hannah from security, audit and evidence owner.
[00:25] Evan Myers: Evan, ML engineer — we build the inference workflows.
[00:28] Jordan Ellis: Great. Marcus, Priya — quick intros.
[00:31] Marcus Chen: Marcus, SE, I focus on private deployments and update mechanics.
[00:33] Priya Nair: Priya, solutions engineering, will cover signing and compliance hooks.
[00:36] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Cool. Samir, we sent a short pre-call doc about hardware — anything to add?
[00:42] Samir Patel: Only that we have limited NVMe tier on older racks, and procurement cycles mean we might not get H100s until Q4. Also, network to the secure facility is intentionally disconnected, so any updates must be delivered via removable media or a locked transfer node.
[00:52] Marcus Chen: Understood. That's typical. We support two offline update patterns: (1) signed image bundles you pull via a transfer appliance, or (2) delta patch packages that apply to an existing image. With limited NVMe we lean toward smaller deltas.
[01:05] Hannah Cho: How do you ensure image integrity? We need cryptographic proof for chain-of-custody.
[01:09] Priya Nair: We use image signing with a customer-managed root of trust option. Redwood can sign artifacts if customers prefer, but in air-gapped mode we recommend customers host the root key, or HSM/KMS integration. The update package includes a signature manifest and a verification step before any write to local storage.
[01:22] Evan Myers: What formats are those patches? Are they container layers, filesystem diffs, or model weights only?
[01:26] Marcus Chen: We support multiple payload types — full VM/container images, model-only weight updates (e.g., delta quantized weights), and a binary patch format our runtime applies. For small NVMe, model-only deltas + streaming from the network attached cache during inference is an option.
[01:41] Dr. Lena Ortiz: We can't stream from external caches, everything must live locally.
[01:45] Jordan Ellis: Right, so we'd aim for minimal footprint on disk, unpack into a working directory, and have a strict atomic swap to reduce window where broken state could exist.
[01:55] Samir Patel: How long does an atomic swap take? We have tight maintenance windows on our clinical nodes — typically 30 to 45 minutes.
[02:02] Marcus Chen: That depends on model size and decompression. For a 7B model with q4 quantization, end-to-end apply can be under 12 minutes on an A100. On older GPUs with slower NVMe it could be longer. We can pre-validate the bundle on a staging node to reduce downtime on the production node.
[02:18] Evan Myers: Pre-validation sounds good. Can we also test a fallback — say a lower precision quantized variant if the new image fails?
[02:23] Priya Nair: Absolutely. Rollouts can be configured with a local fallback policy. For example, if the runtime fails health checks post-swap, we auto-rollback to last known good quantized variant. That logic runs locally so it doesn't need a control plane call-home.
[02:36] Hannah Cho: Audit logs: does Redwood produce tamper-evident logs we can ingest into our SIEM?
[02:41] Marcus Chen: Yes, logs are exported as signed JSON blobs, and we support pushing to a local syslog agent or writing to an append-only audit folder. We can also produce a signed proof-of-installation that includes digest of the installed artifact and timestamp.
[02:55] Samir Patel: About KMS: we use an on-prem HSM. Can Redwood integrate for key wrapping or is it always Redwood-managed?
[03:02] Priya Nair: We have multiple modes: Redwood-managed KMS, customer-managed KMS where we integrate with their HSM via key-wrapping APIs, or a hybrid where keys never leave the HSM. For air-gapped sites, the recommended pattern is to manage the root key in the HSM and provision ephemeral signing keys to a transfer node via an operator-led ceremony.
[03:20] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Ceremony meaning manual operator? That's acceptable but we need a clear runbook.
[03:25] Jordan Ellis: We'll provide an operator runbook that covers the exact steps: key export policy, image signing, transfer media checksum, and installation verification — with checkboxes for auditors.
[03:36] Evan Myers: On the hardware side, our fleet has mixed GPUs: some V100s, a few T4s, and we'll get A100s next quarter. How does Redwood handle model variants across heterogeneous GPUs?
[03:47] Marcus Chen: We recommend shipping supported quantized variants matched to architecture: int8/q4nv for older cards can keep memory down. The runtime can auto-select the best variant if multiple are present. For older GPUs and limited memory we may recommend more aggressive quantization or smaller context windows.
[04:02] Samir Patel: Are there licensing or runtime-agent footprints? We cannot run a constantly phone-home agent.
[04:07] Priya Nair: The agent can be run in fully offline mode; it only needs connectivity during initial artifact staging if you choose Redwood-hosted signing. We can provide a minimal runtime binary and libraries — footprint under 80MB — and all telemetry can be disabled.
[04:21] Hannah Cho: OK, telemetry must be off by default. Also need to see SOC2 artifacts and penetration test results.
[04:27] Jordan Ellis: We'll attach the SOC2 report and a redacted pen-test summary; we can also provide network diagrams and whitepapers describing our offline mode.
[04:35] Dr. Lena Ortiz: What about patch cadence? We have strict validation protocols; we can't accept weekly churn.
[04:41] Marcus Chen: Typical commercial customers choose monthly security patches and quarterly model updates, but the cadence is configurable. We can do a canary on a non-critical rack first, then a staggered rollout. For you, given the clinical impact, a quarterly cadence with emergency hotfixes only seems reasonable.
[04:57] Evan Myers: For validation, can we run Redwood-produced test vectors locally to validate behavior before promoting to prod?
[05:03] Priya Nair: Yes, we can bundle an evaluation harness along with the artifact — includes test prompts, expected ranges, and a scoring script. That can run in your staging environment and produce a verification report.
[05:16] Samir Patel: How do we handle rollback if an update corrupts the model store? Is there a safe copy approach?
[05:22] Marcus Chen: We maintain a last-known-good snapshot. The install process writes to a new directory and uses an atomic symlink swap; if health checks fail, the runtime switches back to the old symlink. That avoids in-place corruption.
[05:35] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Good. Are any components requiring kernel modules or privileged host changes?
[05:41] Marcus Chen: No kernel modules required. The runtime runs user-space, containerized or direct. For performance on some cards we do use vendor drivers but no additional kernel-level hooks.
[05:52] Hannah Cho: Regarding operator access: we want RBAC and SSO for any management UI that might be used from within the secure network.
[05:58] Priya Nair: In Private deployments the control plane can be customer-hosted; we support SAML SSO and external LDAP. For air-gapped installations the management UI is optional and can be operated from a bastion host with local accounts. RBAC can be configured to meet least-privilege.
[06:12] Jordan Ellis: Quick commercial note: Dedicated pricing assumes networked datacenter. Air-gapped Private is billed as an enterprise license + professional services for the initial on-site onboarding and image signing tooling. We can follow up with a tailored quote.
[06:26] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Likely we'll need professional services for the first two on-site installs. What's the typical timeline for an initial air-gapped deployment?
[06:33] Marcus Chen: On-site prep and initial install is typically 2-3 days for a single facility, plus a week for integration and validation. If you want image signing/HSM ceremony support, add an extra day.
[06:45] Evan Myers: For quantization suggestions, can Redwood provide recommended profiles per model size and GPU type?
[06:50] Marcus Chen: Yes, Marcus will produce a compatibility spreadsheet with recommended quant profiles and expected throughput/latency ranges for V100/T4/A100.
[06:59] Samir Patel: One more practical — removable media: do you have a checksum/manifest verifier we can use before ingestion?
[07:04] Priya Nair: The runbook includes a verification script that checks artifacts, manifests, and signature chain. We also recommend using signed checksum tokens to guard transfer media.
[07:14] Hannah Cho: We will need a documented operator checklist for auditors.
[07:18] Jordan Ellis: We'll include a checklist with evidentiary items and sample signed logs.
[07:24] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Great. Any concerns about model drift or quality regressions during quantization? We need to see evaluation thresholds.
[07:31] Priya Nair: We'll include example evals and regression thresholds. Redwood Optimize can run offline evaluations too — we can provide a zipped eval harness for you to run locally.
[07:42] Evan Myers: If we find regression, what's the rollback SLA?
[07:45] Marcus Chen: Rollback is immediate upon failed health check — the runtime reverts. For human-driven rollback we target under 30 minutes from operator start to completion for typical models.
[07:56] Samir Patel: Are there any dependencies that require outbound network access for license checks?
[08:00] Jordan Ellis: No. For air-gapped private installs we do not require outbound license calls. License is baked into the artifact bundle or validated via an offline license token.
[08:09] Dr. Lena Ortiz: OK, this is all helpful. Let's recap and confirm next steps.
[08:14] Jordan Ellis: Recap: Redwood will send an air-gap runbook, HW compatibility spreadsheet with quantization notes, SOC2 and pen-test summaries, and a test artifact for staging. Wintergreen will share approved hardware SKUs, patch window policy, and operator availability for on-site. We'll target an on-site workshop week of 6/14 and provide a quote for professional services.
[08:34] Hannah Cho: That's right. Also please include the signed-logs sample and the verification script.
[08:38] Jordan Ellis: Will do. Anything else?
[08:40] Dr. Lena Ortiz: No, thanks. Good session.
[08:43] Jordan Ellis: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up by Friday with docs and the staging artifact.
[08:47] (crosstalk and meeting wrap)
notes: Customer emphasized strict offline-only rules, limited NVMe and mixed older GPU fleet, and need for operator-run ceremonies and audit-ready artifacts. Redwood committed to runbook, HW matrix, staging artifact, and scheduling an on-site workshop. Telemetry disabled and KMS/HSM integration supported.
